title: Managing Late Afternoon Agitation and Sundowning
content: Ensure adequate daytime lighting and reduce shadows as dusk approaches. Establish a predictable late afternoon routine. Limit caffeine and daytime napping after 2:00 PM. Soothing familiar music or sensory calming activities before twilight significantly reduce evening disorientation.

title: Validation vs. Confrontation in Memory Loss
content: Avoid arguing or correcting reality when the person expresses delusional beliefs (e.g. looking for deceased parents). Use validation therapy: acknowledge the feeling behind the statement ('You must miss your mother very much, tell me about her') rather than asserting that the parent passed away years ago.

title: Overcoming Bathing and Shower Resistance
content: Bathing can feel overwhelming and vulnerable. Ensure the room is warm before entering. Keep the person covered with a dry towel while washing parts of the body. Try gentle music and explain each step calmly before doing it. Consider a sponge bath if water spray causes sensory distress.

title: Wandering Prevention and Safe Environments
content: Wandering often stems from an unmet physical need (hunger, thirst, needing the toilet) or an urge to 'go to work'. Place stop signs or child-safe covers on exit doors. Keep shoes and coats out of plain sight. Ensure daytime physical exercise to promote restful sleep.

title: Caregiver Burden, Respite and Emotional Health
content: Caregiver stress is a recognized clinical concern. Caregivers who experience persistent exhaustion, guilt, or despair should request respite support. Taking even a 30-minute break daily reduces chronic burnout. Connecting with caregiver peer groups significantly reduces isolation.

title: Dysphagia and Medication Swallowing Safety
content: If the person coughs while taking tablets or meals, ensure they sit upright at 90 degrees for at least 30 minutes post-dose. Never crush medications without pharmacist confirmation, as enteric-coated or sustained-release tablets can cause toxicity if pulverized.

title: Responding to Repetitive Questions and Accusations
content: When asked the same question repeatedly, remember that the person's short-term memory buffer is damaged; to them, each time is the first time. Keep answers short, calm, and identical. Redirect attention to a tactile or engaging task (folding napkins, listening to a favorite radio song).
